Every principle, practice & pattern.
And when to reach for each.

A curated field guide to software engineering’s named knowledge: foundational principles, laws and maxims, pragmatic tactics, defensive practices, design patterns classic and modern, architecture, delivery discipline, and the anti-patterns and rethinks that keep the canon honest. It spans Turing’s 1936 limit to the AI-era evidence of 2026, and lineage links weave every entry into one chronological graph.

How to read this page. Definitions and origins follow the linked sources, retrieved and verified 11 July 2026. The Use when / Watch out lines are editorial synthesis: judgment, not citation. Lineage links between cards are synthesis too, except where the later work cites the earlier one. Press / to search, filter with the category pills, and flip the List·Chrono toggle for the time-ordered graph view. No finite catalog is complete; this one aims to cover what practitioners actually name and reach for.

Principles

The load-bearing ideas beneath everything else. Reach for a principle when you feel friction (duplication, rigidity, surprise) and let it name the fix. Applied speculatively, most of them invert into over-engineering.

SOLID

Single Responsibility Principle

Robert C. Martin · 2000 · acronym coined by Michael Feathers (~2004)

“There should never be more than one reason for a class to change.” Each module answers to one actor, one axis of change.

Use when a class keeps changing for unrelated reasons, or two teams keep editing the same file.

Watch out over-splitting into anemic fragments; ‘one responsibility’ means one reason to change, not one method.

SOLID · Wikipedia
Builds on High Cohesion, Low Coupling Challenged by CUPID over SOLID

Open–Closed Principle

Bertrand Meyer 1988 · restated by Robert C. Martin 2000

“Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification”: add behavior via new code, not by editing stable code.

Use when a module has stabilized and variations keep arriving; expose an extension point instead of another if-branch.

Watch out speculative extension points nobody uses; YAGNI applies to abstractions too.

SOLID · Wikipedia
Challenged by CUPID over SOLID

Liskov Substitution Principle

Barbara Liskov 1987 · in SOLID via Martin 2000

Code using a base type must work, unknowingly, with any subtype; subtypes may not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions.

Use when designing any inheritance or interface hierarchy; it is the test for whether ‘is-a’ is real.

Watch out the classic square-extends-rectangle trap; if a subtype throws where the parent didn’t, it isn’t a subtype.

SOLID · Wikipedia
Challenged by CUPID over SOLID

Interface Segregation Principle

Robert C. Martin · 2000

“Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use”: many small role interfaces beat one fat one.

Use when implementers stub out methods with ‘not supported’, or a change in one client’s methods recompiles all of them.

Watch out an interface per method is noise; segregate along real client roles.

SOLID · Wikipedia
Challenged by CUPID over SOLID

Dependency Inversion Principle

Robert C. Martin · 2000

High-level policy and low-level detail both depend on abstractions; policy never imports detail directly.

Use when business logic needs testing without databases, queues, or clocks; invert so the core owns the interface.

Watch out don’t confuse with dependency injection (a technique); DIP is about which direction the source dependency points.

SOLID · Wikipedia
Builds on Program to an Interface, not an Implementation Challenged by CUPID over SOLID

Simplicity

DRY: Don’t Repeat Yourself

Hunt & Thomas · The Pragmatic Programmer · 1999

Every piece of knowledge should have a single, authoritative representation in the system.

Use when the same business rule lives in two places and they have already drifted once.

Watch out DRY is about knowledge, not lines; deduplicating code that merely looks alike couples things that change separately.

DRY · Wikipedia
Leads to AHA: Avoid Hasty Abstractions

KISS: Keep It Simple

Folk engineering maxim · framed for software in Raymond’s Art of Unix Programming (2003)

Prefer the simplest design that meets the need; complexity is spent, not free.

Use when choosing between a working boring design and a clever general one: default to boring.

Watch out simple for the reader, not the writer; a terse one-liner can be the opposite of simple.

Unix philosophy · Wikipedia
Builds on The Unix Philosophy

YAGNI: You Aren’t Gonna Need It

Extreme Programming (Beck/Jeffries) · documented by Fowler

Don’t build capability for presumed future needs; build it when the need is real, and design so it can be added later.

Use when someone says ‘while we’re in here, let’s also support…’; cost of carry beats cost of later addition surprisingly often.

Watch out YAGNI covers features and flexibility, not quality; it is not a license to skip tests or error handling.

Yagni · Fowler blikiYAGNI · Wikipedia
Builds on Do the Simplest Thing That Could Possibly Work Leads to Speculative Generality

AHA: Avoid Hasty Abstractions

Kent C. Dodds · after Sandi Metz’s “wrong abstraction”

Prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction; optimize for change first, and abstract only when the shape of the commonality is proven.

Use when tempted to unify two similar-looking code paths that serve different masters; wait for the third case.

Watch out the counterweight to DRY, not its replacement; genuinely shared knowledge should still live once.

AHA Programming · Dodds
Builds on DRY: Don’t Repeat Yourself, Rule of Three

Rule of Three

Refactoring folklore · recorded in Fowler’s Refactoring

Tolerate a duplication twice; on the third occurrence, refactor; three real uses reveal the true shape of an abstraction.

Use when deciding the moment to extract a helper, a base type, or a service.

Watch out three trivial repeats of one line may never need extracting; three copies of a business rule needed extracting yesterday.

Refactoring · Fowler
Leads to AHA: Avoid Hasty Abstractions

Object design

Composition over Inheritance

GoF · Design Patterns · 1994

“Favor object composition over class inheritance”: assemble behavior from parts held by reference rather than inherited from parents.

Use when behavior needs mixing, swapping, or configuring at runtime; inheritance would fork a combinatorial class tree.

Watch out inheritance is still right for true, stable is-a relationships with LSP intact.

Design principles from Design Patterns · Gamma interviewpython-patterns.guide
Builds on The Gang of Four Catalog Leads to The Banana, the Gorilla, and the Jungle

Program to an Interface, not an Implementation

GoF · Design Patterns · 1994

Depend on the contract a thing exposes, never on the concrete type behind it; callers stay ignorant of construction and class.

Use when any seam you may need to substitute: persistence, transport, formatting, time.

Watch out interfaces with a single forever-only implementation are ceremony; add the seam when a second implementation (including a fake) exists.

Design principles from Design Patterns · Gamma interview
Builds on The Gang of Four Catalog Leads to Dependency Inversion Principle, Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters), Dependency Injection & the Composition Root

Command–Query Separation

Bertrand Meyer · Object-Oriented Software Construction

Queries return a result and change nothing observable; commands change state and return nothing. Asking a question shouldn’t change the answer.

Use when designing any API; it makes reads freely composable and mutations easy to audit.

Watch out pragmatic exceptions exist (pop, compare-and-swap, id-returning inserts); deviate deliberately, not accidentally.

CQS · Fowler bliki
Leads to CQRS

Law of Demeter

Karl Lieberherr et al. · Northeastern · 1987

Principle of least knowledge: talk only to your immediate collaborators, no reaching through objects (a.b().c().d()).

Use when train-wreck call chains appear, or a change in one class ripples through strangers that merely traversed it.

Watch out doesn’t apply to data (JSON, DTOs, fluent builders); it’s about behavioral coupling, not dots.

Law of Demeter · LieberherrWikipedia
Builds on High Cohesion, Low Coupling

Principle of Least Astonishment

Long-standing usability/API maxim

A component should behave the way its name, signature, and context lead people to expect; surprise is a defect.

Use when naming things, choosing defaults, designing side effects: if users would be astonished, redesign.

Watch out the audience defines astonishment: match the conventions of your language and domain, not your private taste.

WikipediaDevIQ

Modularity

Information Hiding

David Parnas · CACM · 1972

Decompose systems around difficult or likely-to-change design decisions and hide each inside a module, not around the steps of a flowchart.

Use when drawing any module boundary: ask ‘what decision does this hide?’, not ‘what step does this perform?’.

Watch out a module whose internals every caller knows hides nothing, whatever its folder structure says.

Parnas 1972 · ACMThe Morning Paper summary
Leads to High Cohesion, Low Coupling, Deep Modules

High Cohesion, Low Coupling

Stevens, Myers & Constantine · Structured Design · 1974

Keep related things together (cohesion) and unrelated things apart (coupling); the oldest quantitative lens on module quality.

Use when evaluating any decomposition: classes, services, teams; most architecture advice is this principle wearing a costume.

Watch out optimizing either alone is easy and useless; one giant module has perfect coupling and terrible cohesion.

A brief history of coupling & cohesionCoupling · Wikipedia
Builds on Information Hiding Leads to Single Responsibility Principle, Law of Demeter, GRASP: Nine Responsibility Principles, Domain-Driven Boundaries (Subdomains & Contexts)

Deep Modules

John Ousterhout · A Philosophy of Software Design · 2018

The best modules have simple interfaces hiding substantial functionality, like Unix file I/O: five calls masking enormous machinery.

Use when judging a design: prefer one deep module over many shallow pass-through classes and wrappers.

Watch out ‘classitis’: decomposition that multiplies interfaces faster than it hides complexity and makes systems shallower.

Ousterhout talk notesPragmatic Engineer interview
Builds on Information Hiding Leads to Define Errors Out of Existence

Easy to Use Correctly, Hard to Use Incorrectly

Scott Meyers · IEEE Software · 2004

Meyers’ candidate for the most important design guideline: interfaces should make the right usage the path of least resistance and misuse a compile error.

Use when every public API: constrain types, order, and defaults so mistakes don’t fit through the signature.

Watch out documentation is not a fix for an interface that invites misuse.

The Most Important Design Guideline · Meyers

Design by Contract

Bertrand Meyer · Eiffel · 1980s

Specify each routine’s preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants as executable obligations between caller and callee.

Use when correctness-critical modules; contracts double as documentation, runtime checks, and test oracles.

Watch out checks that vanish in production remove the safety net exactly where it matters; decide deliberately what stays on.

Design by Contract · EiffelWikipedia
Leads to Assertions in Anger, NASA’s Power of 10

GRASP: Nine Responsibility Principles

Craig Larman · Applying UML and Patterns · 1997

Information Expert, Creator, Controller, Low Coupling, High Cohesion, Polymorphism, Indirection, Pure Fabrication, Protected Variations: a checklist for assigning responsibilities to classes.

Use when deciding where behavior lives: give the job to whoever has the information (Expert), and wrap instability behind interfaces (Protected Variations).

Watch out a thinking tool, not an architecture; don’t manufacture Controllers and Fabrications where a function would do.

GRASP · Wikipedia
Builds on High Cohesion, Low Coupling

Composition

The Unix Philosophy

Doug McIlroy · Bell Labs · documented 1978

“Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface.”

Use when CLI tools, pipelines, microservices: anywhere small sharp tools composed loosely beat one integrated giant.

Watch out composition pushes complexity into the glue; a pipeline of ten clever filters is its own big program.

Unix philosophy · Wikipedia
Leads to KISS: Keep It Simple, The Zen of Python, Middleware Pipelines

The Zen of Python

Tim Peters · PEP 20 · 2004

Nineteen aphorisms: explicit is better than implicit, simple is better than complex, errors should never pass silently, there should be one obvious way to do it.

Use when language-agnostic taste calibration; ‘errors should never pass silently’ alone justifies the read.

Watch out aphorisms conflict by design; ‘practicality beats purity’ is in there to keep the rest honest.

PEP 20
Builds on The Unix Philosophy

Laws & Maxims

Named observations about how software and the people who build it actually behave. Laws don’t tell you what to do; they tell you what will happen anyway, so you can design for it.

Foundations

Turing's Limit (Undecidability)

Alan Turing · “On Computable Numbers” · 1936

Turing's machines and the halting problem: no general procedure can decide what an arbitrary program will do. Every static analyzer, dead-code detector, and bug-finder lives under this ceiling.

Use when whenever a tool promises to find all bugs or prove arbitrary properties: the limit is mathematical, so real tools approximate, restrict the language, or ask you for annotations.

Watch out undecidable in general is not hopeless in practice: bounded loops and restricted idioms (see Power of 10) exist precisely to make analysis tractable.

On Computable Numbers (PDF)Halting problem · Wikipedia
Leads to NASA’s Power of 10

The Stored-Program Computer

John von Neumann · First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC · 1945

Program and data share one memory: code is data. The architecture beneath compilers, interpreters, and serialization, and equally beneath every injection attack ever written.

Use when code-is-data cuts both ways: it enables toolchains and metaprogramming, and it is why untrusted data must never be allowed to become executable.

Watch out the famous draft's sole authorship is contested (Eckert and Mauchly's engineering fed it); the same architecture also named the CPU-memory bottleneck.

First Draft on the EDVAC · WikipediaVon Neumann architecture
Leads to Parameterized Queries

Information Theory

Claude Shannon · A Mathematical Theory of Communication · 1948

Shannon quantified information (the bit), channel capacity, and redundancy: the mathematics beneath compression, checksums, hashing, and every noisy channel your systems talk over.

Use when reasoning about compression limits, checksum strength, and the entropy of identifiers and secrets; password strength is Shannon entropy wearing a product name.

Watch out information is not meaning: the theory prices bits, not sense, and nothing in it says your log pipeline carries anything worth knowing.

A Mathematical Theory of Communication (PDF)Wikipedia
Leads to Design for Error (Hamming Codes)

Design for Error (Hamming Codes)

Richard Hamming · Bell System Technical Journal · 1950

The first error-correcting codes: assume corruption will happen and add structured redundancy so the system detects and repairs it in flight. The defensive stance, decades before defensive programming had a name.

Use when the ancestor mindset of ECC memory, checksums, RAID, and retries: budget redundancy in proportion to what you cannot afford to lose.

Watch out redundancy corrects noise, not bugs: a bad write replicated three times is three bad copies, which is why replication is not backup.

Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes (PDF)Hamming code · Wikipedia
Builds on Information Theory

Another Level of Indirection

Attributed to David Wheeler · Cambridge

“All problems in computer science can be solved by another level of indirection”: the folklore fundamental theorem of software engineering, with its equally canonical corollary about the problem of too many levels of indirection.

Use when pointers, virtual dispatch, adapters, gateways, dependency injection: every decoupling trick on this page is an indirection with a better name.

Watch out each level costs comprehension and latency; indirection you cannot justify is architecture-flavored debt.

Indirection · WikipediaDavid Wheeler · Wikipedia

People & organizations

Conway’s Law

Melvin Conway · “How Do Committees Invent?” · 1968

Organizations design systems that mirror their communication structures; the org chart ships.

Use when planning architecture: align team boundaries with intended service boundaries (the ‘inverse Conway maneuver’), or the system will realign itself.

Watch out it cuts both ways: reorganizing without re-architecting leaves the old structure fossilized in code.

Conway’s Law · melconway.comWikipedia
Leads to Domain-Driven Boundaries (Subdomains & Contexts), Monolith First, Microservices Maybe

Hyrum’s Law

Hyrum Wright · Google · named by Titus Winters

“With a sufficient number of users of an API, it does not matter what you promise in the contract: all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody.”

Use when changing anything observable (timing, ordering, error text) on a widely used surface; assume someone depends on it.

Watch out not an excuse to freeze forever: it argues for deliberate contracts, deprecation windows, and tooling to find dependents.

hyrumslaw.com

Brooks: No Silver Bullet

Fred Brooks · 1986

Software difficulty divides into essence (the problem’s inherent complexity) and accident (our tools’ friction); no single technique will yield an order-of-magnitude gain, because essence remains.

Use when evaluating any tool or method promising 10×: ask whether it attacks essence or only accident.

Watch out written before modern tooling, still holding; but ‘no silver bullet’ is not ‘no progress’; accidents are worth removing.

No Silver Bullet · WikipediaOriginal paper (PDF)
Builds on Second-System Effect

Systems

Gall’s Law

John Gall · Systemantics · 1975

“A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked… A complex system designed from scratch never works.”

Use when tempted by a big-bang design or rewrite: start with the smallest working system and grow it.

Watch out the corollary bites rewrites hardest; see Strangler Fig for the escape hatch.

John Gall · WikiquoteSystemantics · Wikipedia
Leads to Monolith First, Microservices Maybe, Strangler Fig

Postel’s Law and Its Modern Reversal

Jon Postel · RFC 761 · revisited by IAB RFC 9413 (2023)

“Be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept”, now formally reconsidered: RFC 9413 finds liberal acceptance breeds a “pathological feedback cycle” where bugs entrench into de-facto protocol.

Use when reading old advice: today, prefer strict validation with clear errors (“virtuous intolerance”) and actively maintained specs.

Watch out strictness needs a feedback channel: reject loudly and legibly, or you just moved the pain.

RFC 9413Robustness principle · Wikipedia
Challenged by Schema Validation at Trust Boundaries, Input Validation & Output Encoding

CAP Theorem

Eric Brewer conjecture 2000 · proved by Gilbert & Lynch 2002

Under a network partition, a distributed system must sacrifice either consistency or availability; you cannot have all three of C, A, P.

Use when choosing a datastore or replication mode: decide per operation what yields during partitions: stale reads or refused writes.

Watch out partitions are rare; the everyday trade-off is latency vs. consistency. ‘CP vs AP’ labels oversimplify real systems.

Gilbert & Lynch proof (PDF)CAP · Wikipedia
Builds on The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing

The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing

Peter Deutsch et al. · Sun Microsystems · 1994

The network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite; the network is secure; topology doesn’t change; there is one administrator; transport cost is zero; the network is homogeneous. All false.

Use when reviewing any design with a network hop in it; each fallacy maps to a required defense (timeouts, retries, idempotency, TLS…).

Watch out the fallacies apply inside ‘one’ system too: microservices turn function calls into all eight problems.

WikipediaUnpacking the fallacies · Sookocheff
Leads to CAP Theorem, Timeouts, Retries & Backoff with Jitter, Circuit Breaker, Idempotency & Idempotency Keys, Service Discovery, Patterns of Distributed Systems, Distributed Monolith

Hoare’s Billion-Dollar Mistake

Tony Hoare · QCon London · 2009

Hoare calls his 1965 invention of the null reference “my billion-dollar mistake”, a decade-spanning source of crashes and vulnerabilities.

Use when motivation for Option/Maybe types, null-safety analysis, and non-nullable-by-default languages.

Watch out banning null locally while accepting it at boundaries just relocates the crash; convert at the edge.

InfoQ talk
Leads to Model Absence Explicitly (Option/Maybe)

Craft

Knuth: Premature Optimization

Donald Knuth · “Structured Programming with go to Statements” · 1974

“Premature optimization is the root of all evil”. In context: forget small efficiencies ~97% of the time, but do not pass up the critical 3%, found by measurement.

Use when resisting micro-optimization before profiling; and equally, justifying real optimization once a profile names the hot path.

Watch out the quote is not an amnesty for wasteful architecture; asymptotics and data layout chosen up front are design, not premature tuning.

Revisiting Knuth’s paper · Probably DanceContext · hlopko
Leads to Measure First

Make It Work, Make It Right, Make It Fast

Attributed to Kent Beck · older roots in the folklore

Sequence your effort: first a working thing, then a clean correct thing, then (only if needed and measured) a fast thing.

Use when a standing antidote to designing for performance before correctness, or polishing before anything works end-to-end.

Watch out ‘make it work’ is not license to ship the prototype; the second step is the point.

Origin discussion · BourguignonAgile in a Flash

Worse Is Better

Richard P. Gabriel · 1989–91

Gabriel’s observation that ‘New Jersey style’ (simple implementation, even at some interface cost) spreads and survives better than ‘MIT style’ perfect design.

Use when strategy calls: shipping a simple 80% solution that can spread beats polishing a complete one that can’t.

Watch out a description of evolutionary dynamics, not a quality target; Gabriel himself argued both sides for years.

Worse Is Better · DreamsongsWikipedia
Leads to Choose Boring Technology

Choose Boring Technology

Dan McKinley · 2015

Every team holds a handful of ‘innovation tokens’; spend them on your core problem and choose well-understood, operationally boring tech for everything else.

Use when picking databases, queues, frameworks: the failure modes of boring tech are documented; novel tech fails novelly at 3 a.m.

Watch out boring ≠ obsolete; the point is known failure modes, and tokens exist to be spent, deliberately.

Choose Boring Technology · McKinley
Builds on Worse Is Better

Chesterton’s Fence

G. K. Chesterton’s parable · adopted by software

Don’t remove a fence until you know why it was put up: code you can’t explain is not yet code you may delete.

Use when before deleting ‘dead’ checks, odd sleeps, weird special cases: git blame and tests first, then remove with confidence.

Watch out not a ban on cleanup; once you know why it exists (or that the reason is gone), remove it boldly.

SymflowerJoseph Woodward

The Two Hard Things

Phil Karlton · via Fowler’s bliki

“There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.” The joke endures because both are about keeping two representations honestly in sync.

Use when as a smell detector: every cache you add is a consistency problem you now own; every bad name is a small lie readers must unlearn.

Watch out the extended joke adds off-by-one errors; treat all three as budget items, not punchlines.

Two Hard Things · Fowlerkarlton.org

Pragmatism & Tactics

Judgment under real constraints: the Pragmatic Programmer’s craft ethos, XP’s small brave moves, and the process wisdom teams learn the hard way. Perfection isn’t the goal here; deliberate, reversible progress is.

Pragmatic craft

The Pragmatic Programmer Ethos

Andrew Hunt & David Thomas · 1999 / 20th-anniv. 2019

Care about your craft and think about your work: take responsibility (“provide options, don’t make lame excuses”), invest in your knowledge portfolio, and be a catalyst for change: stone-soup style, show a taste of what’s possible.

Use when the operating system for everything tactical below; the book’s 100 tips are a career-long checklist.

Watch out pragmatism means judgment, not shortcuts; the same book demands DRY, contracts, and ruthless testing.

Pragmatic Programmer tips20th Anniversary Edition
Leads to No Broken Windows, Tracer Bullets, Rubber Duck Debugging, “select” Isn’t Broken

No Broken Windows

Hunt & Thomas · The Pragmatic Programmer

“Don’t live with broken windows”: visible neglect (bad designs, wrong decisions, poor code left unfixed) normalizes decay and invites more. Fix small rot fast, or at least board it up visibly.

Use when triaging small messes: the cost of the fix is rarely the point; the signal to the team is.

Watch out the inverse holds too: pristine codebases stay pristine because nobody wants to be the first window.

Pragmatic Programmer tipsQuick reference
Builds on The Pragmatic Programmer Ethos

Good-Enough Software

Ed Yourdon · IEEE Software 1995 · adopted by the Pragmatic Programmer

“Make quality a requirements issue”: involve users in deciding the quality/scope/time trade-off deliberately, and know when to stop polishing; great software today often beats perfect software next year.

Use when scoping real releases; ‘good enough’ is a negotiated, explicit bar, not whatever shipped.

Watch out this is about trade-offs the user chose, never silent corner-cutting; undisclosed ‘good enough’ is just bad.

When Good Enough Software Is Best · Yourdon (ACM)Pragmatic Programmer tips

Tracer Bullets

Hunt & Thomas · The Pragmatic Programmer

“Use tracer bullets to find the target”: build a thin but real end-to-end slice through every layer first, then thicken it under continuous feedback. Unlike a prototype, tracer code is kept.

Use when new systems with unknowns in every layer; the skeleton proves the architecture while there’s still time to aim differently.

Watch out distinguish from spikes/prototypes: those are for learning and get thrown away; tracer code must meet production standards.

Pragmatic Programmer tipsQuick reference
Builds on The Pragmatic Programmer Ethos Leads to Walking Skeleton

Rubber Duck Debugging

Popularized by The Pragmatic Programmer · 1999

Explain the code line by line to someone (or something) that can’t answer. Verbalizing forces the assumptions into the open, where the wrong one becomes obvious.

Use when stuck past the fifteen-minute mark; the duck works because articulation is the debugger.

Watch out if explaining it aloud doesn’t crack it, write it down: a good bug report to a colleague is the duck’s final form.

Rubber duck debugging · Wikipedia
Builds on The Pragmatic Programmer Ethos

“select” Isn’t Broken

Hunt & Thomas · via Atwood’s “It’s Always Your Fault”

When you’re sure the compiler, OS, or library is buggy: it isn’t. The bug is in your code, statistically and overwhelmingly. Suspect yourself first and prove it with a minimal case.

Use when any ‘impossible’ bug; the discipline of assuming your own fault finds it faster than the conspiracy theory does.

Watch out platform bugs do exist; earn that conclusion with a reduced reproduction, then file it upstream properly.

It’s Always Your Fault · Coding Horror
Builds on The Pragmatic Programmer Ethos

Tactical moves

Do the Simplest Thing That Could Possibly Work

Ward Cunningham & Kent Beck · XP

When unsure how to proceed, ask what the simplest thing that could possibly work is; then do that, and let real feedback drive the next elaboration.

Use when paralyzed between three clever designs: the simple one teaches you which of the others you actually need.

Watch out ‘could possibly work’ still means work; it’s a discipline against speculation, not against thinking.

c2 wikiCunningham interview · artima
Leads to YAGNI: You Aren’t Gonna Need It, Test-Driven Development, Spike Solution

Spike Solution

Extreme Programming · extremeprogramming.org

A small, timeboxed, throwaway experiment to answer one risky question: explore the unknown, harvest the knowledge, delete the code.

Use when estimating or designing around a technical unknown; an afternoon’s spike beats a week’s debate.

Watch out the discipline is the deletion: a spike that ships is a prototype in production wearing a lab coat.

Spike solution · XP rulesSpike Solutions · Shore
Builds on Do the Simplest Thing That Could Possibly Work Leads to Vibe Coding

Walking Skeleton

Alistair Cockburn · via 97 Things Every Software Architect Should Know

A tiny implementation that performs one small end-to-end function through all architectural layers; built, deployed, and tested first, then grown feature by feature.

Use when project kickoff: it forces the build pipeline, deployment, and integration risks to the front, where they’re cheap.

Watch out keep the skeleton walking: if it can’t deploy green at all times, you’ve lost the point of having it.

Start with a Walking Skeleton · 97 Thingsc2 wiki
Builds on Tracer Bullets

Make the Change Easy, Then Make the Easy Change

Kent Beck · applied as preparatory refactoring (Fowler)

“For each desired change, make the change easy (warning: this may be hard), then make the easy change”: refactor the ground first so the feature lands as a small, obvious diff.

Use when a feature that fights the current structure; the preparatory refactoring ships separately and safely under tests.

Watch out keep the two commits distinct; mixing the restructuring with the behavior change makes both unreviewable.

Preparatory refactoring example · Fowler
Builds on Opportunistic Refactoring & the Boy Scout Rule

Opportunistic Refactoring & the Boy Scout Rule

Robert C. Martin (97 Things) · Martin Fowler (bliki)

“Leave the campground cleaner than you found it”: whenever you touch code, make it a little better (rename the misleading variable, extract the tangled block) as part of the work, not a separate project.

Use when the compounding-interest answer to tech debt: continuous small payments beat rare big refactoring festivals.

Watch out scope discipline: a two-line cleanup is a courtesy, a drive-by rewrite in a feature PR is a review hazard (Chesterton applies).

The Boy Scout Rule · 97 ThingsOpportunistic Refactoring · Fowler
Builds on Technical Debt Leads to Make the Change Easy, Then Make the Easy Change

If It Hurts, Do It More Often

Martin Fowler · “Frequency Reduces Difficulty”

Painful activities (integration, releases, upgrades) hurt in proportion to how rarely you do them: batch size grows, feedback shrinks, skills atrophy. Raising the frequency shrinks each dose until it’s routine.

Use when the logic behind CI, small releases, and dependency-update bots; if a task is dreaded, schedule it weekly, not yearly.

Watch out applies to batchable pain, not all pain; doing a genuinely broken process more often just breaks you more often; fix the process too.

Frequency Reduces Difficulty · Fowler
Leads to Trunk-Based Development

Process wisdom

Technical Debt

Ward Cunningham · OOPSLA 1992 · elaborated by Fowler

Cunningham’s metaphor: shipping with a shortcut is borrowing: fine, like debt is fine, if taken deliberately and repaid; unpaid, the interest (every future change costs more) compounds until progress stalls.

Use when making trade-offs legible to non-engineers: name the loan, record it (an ADR works), schedule the repayment.

Watch out the metaphor covers deliberate, prudent shortcuts; plain sloppiness isn’t debt, it’s vandalism, and calling it debt launders it.

Technical Debt · Fowler blikiIntro to the concept · Agile Alliance (PDF)
Leads to Architecture Decision Records, Opportunistic Refactoring & the Boy Scout Rule

The Agile Manifesto’s Four Values

17 signatories · Snowbird · 2001

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan; “while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.”

Use when the original text is a corrective to ceremony in both directions; reread it whenever ‘agile’ has become a process with more tools than interactions.

Watch out ‘over’ is not ‘instead of’; the right-hand items are explicitly valuable: the manifesto ranks, it doesn’t abolish.

agilemanifesto.org
Challenges Waterfall Was a Warning, Not a Recommendation Leads to DORA’s Four Keys, The Agile Industrial Complex

Second-System Effect

Fred Brooks · The Mythical Man-Month · 1975

“The second is the most dangerous system a man ever designs”: after a disciplined first system, designers unload every deferred embellishment onto its successor, over-engineering it into trouble.

Use when any v2, rewrite, or ‘platform’ project: keep a public list of rejected embellishments and make restraint the explicit goal.

Watch out pairs with Gall’s Law: the safe second system evolves from the working first one instead of replacing it wholesale.

Second-system effect · WikipediaThe Mythical Man-Month · Wikipedia
Leads to Brooks: No Silver Bullet

Law of Triviality (Bikeshedding)

C. Northcote Parkinson · 1957

Groups spend attention in inverse proportion to a topic’s importance: the nuclear plant is approved in minutes, the bike shed’s color takes an hour, because everyone can hold an opinion about the shed.

Use when structuring reviews and RFCs: timebox the trivial, route paint-color decisions to one owner, and spend the meeting on the reactor.

Watch out dismissing a concern as bikeshedding is itself a move in the game; check whether it’s genuinely trivial before wielding the word.

Law of triviality · Wikipedia

Cargo-Cult Programming

Jargon derived from Feynman’s “cargo cult science” (1974)

Ritually including code, patterns, or process because successful projects had them: runways and coconut headsets, no planes. Form without the understanding that made the form work.

Use when as a self-check: for every convention you copy (this annotation, that folder layout, sprints themselves), can you state what breaks without it?

Watch out the cure is Chesterton’s fence run in reverse: learn why the original worked before importing its shape.

Cargo cult programming · WikipediaJargon File

Five Whys

Taiichi Ohno · Toyota Production System

Ask ‘why?’ repeatedly (about five times) to walk from a symptom to a root cause worth fixing: the fuse blew → why → why → the pump lacks a strainer.

Use when incident analysis and stubborn bugs; the fifth why usually lands in process or design, not in the person nearest the failure.

Watch out naive use stops at a comfortable why or picks one causal chain of many; branch when reality branches, and never let it terminate at ‘human error’.

Five whys · Wikipedia5 Whys · Lean Enterprise Institute

Blameless Postmortems

Google SRE Book · postmortem culture

Analyze incidents on the assumption that everyone acted reasonably on the information they had: name the systemic causes, never the operator, because blame buys silence, and silence buys repeat incidents.

Use when after every user-visible incident; the artifact is a written record of causes and prioritized prevention work.

Watch out blameless doesn’t mean consequence-free or vague; it means the ‘why’ chain ends in systems and incentives, not in a scapegoat.

Postmortem Culture · SRE Book
Builds on SRE: Golden Signals, SLOs & Error Budgets

AI-era craft

Prompt Engineering

Canonized by DAIR.AI's Prompt Engineering Guide

The first-wave skill of the LLM era: phrasing instructions, examples, and output formats so a model does what you mean (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought). Canonized in community guides, then demoted from job title to table stakes within three years.

Use when still the atomic layer: every agent turn bottoms out in a prompt, so clarity, worked examples, and explicit output contracts never stopped mattering.

Watch out brittle on its own: most of what looked like prompt problems were context problems, which is exactly why the successor terms exist.

Prompt Engineering Guide · DAIR.AIThe guide's story · Saravia
Leads to Vibe Coding Challenged by Context Engineering

Vibe Coding

Andrej Karpathy · February 2025

Karpathy's coinage: “fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists”. Conversational programming where AI output is accepted wholesale. Willison's useful boundary: if you reviewed and understood the code, that was AI-assisted programming, not vibe coding.

Use when throwaway prototypes, personal tools, and spikes: it is the spike solution reborn, and as with spikes, the discipline is deleting.

Watch out unreviewed code in production is unowned code; a vibe-coded system fails Chesterton's fence by construction, because nobody knows why anything exists.

Karpathy's original postNot all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding · Willison
Builds on Spike Solution, Prompt Engineering Challenges Code Review, the Google Way Challenged by Spec-Driven Development

Context Engineering

Named across 2025 · endorsed by Karpathy

Karpathy: “+1 for context engineering over prompt engineering”, the delicate art and science of filling the context window: retrieval, tools, memory, and structure for industrial-strength LLM systems, replacing prompt-tinkering as the working skill.

Use when building anything agentic: curate what the model sees the way you would onboard a new engineer; the boundary disciplines on this page (schemas, trust, staleness) apply to context verbatim.

Watch out it inherits every information-architecture problem this catalog already names; the buffer is new, the failure modes are not.

Karpathy on context engineeringContext Engineering Guide
Challenges Prompt Engineering Leads to Harness Engineering

Spec-Driven Development

GitHub Spec Kit · 2025

The intent-first corrective to vibe coding: an executable specification drives AI implementation (specify, plan, break into tasks, implement), making the spec the artifact humans review, version, and regenerate code from.

Use when AI-heavy delivery where review cannot keep pace with generation: move human judgment up to the spec, where one decision governs many diffs.

Watch out specs rot exactly like documentation unless they stay executable; this is TDD's oldest lesson wearing 2025 clothes.

Spec-driven development · GitHub bloggithub/spec-kit
Builds on Test-Driven Development Challenges Vibe Coding

Harness Engineering

Named across 2026 · O'Reilly Radar, Osmani, Fowler's site

The scaffolding around the model: tools, permissions, memory, evals, retries, sandboxes, and observability that turn a chat loop into a dependable worker. The 2026 consensus is that the wrapper often drives more performance than the model inside it.

Use when when agent quality plateaus, engineer the harness (what the agent can touch, see, and verify) before shopping for a bigger model.

Watch out a harness is a distributed system wearing a new name: least privilege, timeouts, idempotency, and limits from this canon apply to it verbatim.

Agent Harness Engineering · O'Reilly RadarHarness engineering · martinfowler.com
Builds on Context Engineering, MCP: Model Context Protocol Leads to Loop Engineering

Loop Engineering

Named mid-2026 · the fourth shift after prompt, context, and harness

Designing the agent's iteration itself: plan-act-observe cycles, termination conditions, budgets, checkpoints, and escalation to humans. If the harness is the cage, loop engineering is the choreography inside it.

Use when long-running agents: define what one round must accomplish, what ends the loop, and what evidence each iteration produces; an unbounded agent loop is an outage with an API bill.

Watch out young vocabulary with shifting definitions (as of mid-2026); the durable core is old wisdom, bounded loops and explicit exit conditions.

Demystifying loop engineering · TechTalksThe four shifts · AI Builder Club
Builds on Harness Engineering, Bound Everything

Types & Data

Make the compiler carry proof. Model data so that wrong states don’t exist, absence is explicit, and raw input is converted into trustworthy types exactly once, at the boundary.

Boundaries in the type system

Parse, Don’t Validate

Alexis King · 2019

Validation checks a condition and discards the knowledge; parsing preserves it in the type. Convert raw input into a precise type once, at the boundary, and let only parsed types flow inward.

Use when any external input: JSON, env vars, DB rows, user forms; downstream code should never re-check what a type already proves.

Watch out if a function accepts a raw type and ‘trusts’ it, the proof burden silently returns.

Parse, don’t validate · King
Builds on Make Illegal States Unrepresentable Leads to Total Functions, Schema Validation at Trust Boundaries

Make Illegal States Unrepresentable

Yaron Minsky · Effective ML

Model data with sums and products so that invalid combinations simply cannot be constructed; the compiler enforces the invariant forever.

Use when fields that are ‘only valid together’ or state flags that exclude each other; replace booleans-plus-comments with a union.

Watch out total unrepresentability can over-rigidify evolving domains; keep escape hatches at the edges, not the core.

DevIQMinsky · lecture notes
Builds on Model Absence Explicitly (Option/Maybe) Leads to Parse, Don’t Validate, Branded / Opaque Types, Exhaustiveness Checking

Model Absence Explicitly (Option/Maybe)

Response to Hoare’s null (2009 mea culpa)

Represent ‘may be missing’ as a first-class type the compiler forces you to unwrap, instead of a null that detonates at a distance.

Use when everywhere a value is optional by design; the signature should say so.

Watch out Option-of-Option and optional-everything signal unclear domain rules, not safety.

Hoare · Billion Dollar Mistake
Builds on Hoare’s Billion-Dollar Mistake Leads to Make Illegal States Unrepresentable, Errors as Values (Result / Railway-Oriented)

Branded / Opaque Types

Nominal-typing technique · TS community

Give semantically distinct values distinct types (UserId, not string; Cents, not number) so mix-ups fail at compile time.

Use when IDs, money, units, sanitized strings, validated emails; anywhere two ‘strings’ must never swap.

Watch out brand at the boundary via smart constructors, or the brand is a costume.

Branded Types · Learning TypeScript
Builds on Value Objects & Money, Make Illegal States Unrepresentable Leads to Smart Constructors

Smart Constructors

Typed-FP technique · via Giulio Canti

Make the only way to build a value pass through validation, so possession of the type is proof of its invariants.

Use when pairs with branded types and parse-don’t-validate as the enforcement mechanism.

Watch out keep a single constructor path; a public unchecked constructor next to a smart one defeats both.

Smart constructors · Canti
Builds on Branded / Opaque Types

Total Functions

Typed-FP vocabulary · follows King’s parsing discipline

A total function answers for every input in its declared domain; partiality (failure, absence) must appear in the return type, never as a hidden throw or hang.

Use when library and core code: callers can see everything that can happen in the signature.

Watch out totality by lying (returning a default that hides failure) is worse than honest partiality.

Parse, don’t validate · King
Builds on Parse, Don’t Validate

Exhaustiveness Checking

Discriminated unions + never · TypeScript idiom

End every match over a closed union with a check that fails to compile when a new variant appears; the compiler finds every switch you forgot.

Use when state machines, event types, API result variants; adding a case becomes a guided refactor.

Watch out a default branch that ‘handles’ unknown cases silently disables the whole mechanism.

Narrowing · TS HandbookFullStory · exhaustiveness
Builds on Make Illegal States Unrepresentable

Domain values

Value Objects & Money

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

Small immutable objects whose equality is by value, not identity: dates, ranges, money. PoEAA gives Money its own pattern: amount plus currency, never a bare float.

Use when any quantity with rules (currency, units, precision); the object carries the rules with the number.

Watch out value objects want immutability; a setter on Money is a bug generator.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler
Leads to Branded / Opaque Types, Money Is Integers (or Decimals), Never Binary Floats

Money Is Integers (or Decimals), Never Binary Floats

Industry consensus · Modern Treasury et al.

Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal cents; store minor units as integers or use a decimal type, and round only at defined boundaries.

Use when all monetary storage, arithmetic, and comparison; no exceptions in ledgers.

Watch out division and allocation still need explicit rounding rules (who gets the leftover cent?).

Floats don’t work for cents · Modern Treasury
Builds on Value Objects & Money

Time: UTC, Zones, and Monotonic Clocks

Hard-won folklore · “Falsehoods about time”

Store and compare instants in UTC; attach IANA zones only for humans; measure durations with a monotonic clock; never hand-roll date arithmetic; the falsehoods list exists because everyone does.

Use when scheduling, logging, expiry, benchmarks: anywhere wall clocks can jump, drift, or repeat an hour.

Watch out future events in local civil time are the exception: zones’ rules change, so store intent (time + zone), not the computed instant.

Falsehoods programmers believe about time

Schema Validation at Trust Boundaries

OWASP guidance + runtime schema tools (zod)

Every input crossing a trust boundary (network, env, disk, DB, user) is parsed against an explicit schema on a trusted system, with unknown fields rejected; inside the boundary, code trusts types.

Use when the runtime half of parse-don’t-validate; server-side always, allow-lists over deny-lists.

Watch out validating on the client only is decoration; attackers don’t run your client.

OWASP Secure Coding checklistzod
