Errors & Resilience

Assume failure is normal. Expected failures travel as values; broken invariants stop the program near the cause; every dependency is treated as slow, flaky, and occasionally down.

Failure semantics

Fail Fast

Jim Shore · IEEE Software · 2004

On detecting a problem, fail immediately and visibly near the cause. Working around errors automatically makes software “fail in mysterious ways later on”; failing fast yields fewer defects.

Use when broken invariants, impossible states, bad configuration: stop at the source, don’t limp on with corrupt state.

Watch out fail fast applies to bugs; expected operational failures deserve handling, not crashes; see errors-as-values.

Fail Fast · ShoreIEEE PDF

Errors as Values (Result / Railway-Oriented)

Typed-FP practice · Scott Wlaschin’s ROP

Expected failures travel in the return type (Result/Either) and compose along a ‘failure track’; exceptions are reserved for genuine bugs.

Use when domain operations that can legitimately fail: parsing, lookups, payments; the signature shows every outcome.

Watch out don’t Result-wrap true invariant violations; a corrupted heap is not a value to pass along.

Railway Oriented Programming · Wlaschin
Builds on Model Absence Explicitly (Option/Maybe)

Assertions in Anger

NASA/JPL Power of 10 · TigerBeetle TigerStyle

Average at least two assertions per function; assert arguments, returns, pre/postconditions, invariants, and assert both what you expect and what must never happen.

Use when long-running and safety-critical code; assertions catch bugs at the moment of violation instead of megabytes later.

Watch out never put side effects in assertions, and decide explicitly which checks survive into production builds.

Power of 10 (PDF)TIGER_STYLE.md
Builds on NASA’s Power of 10, Design by Contract

NASA’s Power of 10

Gerard Holzmann · NASA/JPL · IEEE Computer 2006

Ten verifiable rules for safety-critical code: simple control flow (no recursion), fixed loop bounds, no dynamic allocation after init, short functions, ≥2 assertions per function, smallest scope, check every return, minimal preprocessor and pointers, zero warnings at the strictest settings.

Use when embedded and life-critical software literally; everywhere else, as a calibration for how strict ‘strict’ can get.

Watch out written for C at JPL; import the spirit (bounded, checkable, assertion-dense) rather than the letter.

Power of 10 (PDF)Wikipedia
Builds on Design by Contract, Turing's Limit (Undecidability) Leads to Assertions in Anger, TigerStyle, Bound Everything

TigerStyle

TigerBeetle · engineering style guide

A modern descendant of Power of 10: put a limit on everything (all loops and queues bounded), no recursion, assert positive and negative space, smallest scope, all compiler warnings at the strictest setting from day one.

Use when database-grade and financial software; also the best single document to steal defensive defaults from.

Watch out its static-allocation stance assumes a fixed-workload design; adopt the limits mindset even where you keep malloc.

TIGER_STYLE.mdtigerstyle.dev
Builds on NASA’s Power of 10 Leads to Bound Everything

Define Errors Out of Existence

John Ousterhout · A Philosophy of Software Design

Redesign APIs so edge cases are normal behavior (deleting a missing file succeeds, unsetting an unset variable is fine), shrinking the error surface callers must handle.

Use when designing library semantics: every exception you don’t throw is handling code nobody writes wrong.

Watch out don’t define away errors the caller genuinely must know about; silence is only golden when the outcome is truly equivalent.

Ousterhout · talk notes
Builds on Deep Modules

Never Swallow Errors

Standard practice · corollary of fail-fast

No empty catch blocks: every error is handled meaningfully, converted to a typed error with context, or rethrown: one of the three, always.

Use when code review checklist item; empty catches are where production mysteries are born.

Watch out logging alone is usually swallowing with extra steps; the caller still proceeds on a lie.

Fail Fast · Shore

Crash-Only Software

Candea & Fox · HotOS IX · 2003

Design so the only way to stop is to crash and the only way to start is to recover: one code path, exercised constantly, safe to kill at any time.

Use when services under orchestrators that will kill them anyway; makes recovery the tested path rather than the feared one.

Watch out requires idempotent, journaled effects underneath; crash-only with non-idempotent side effects is just crashing.

Crash-Only Software · USENIX

Boundary protection

Anti-Corruption Layer

Eric Evans · DDD · via Azure Architecture Center

A translation layer between your model and a legacy or third-party system, converting their types, semantics, and errors into yours at the border.

Use when integrating anything you don’t control; upstream weirdness stays quarantined at the edge.

Watch out an ACL that leaks upstream types through it is a hallway, not a wall.

ACL · Azure Architecture Center
Builds on Domain-Driven Boundaries (Subdomains & Contexts)

Timeouts, Retries & Backoff with Jitter

Marc Brooker · AWS Builders’ Library

Every remote call gets a timeout chosen from latency data; retries are ‘selfish’, so they are bounded, exponentially backed off, capped, jittered, applied at a single layer, and only on idempotent operations.

Use when every network dependency, no exceptions; unjittered synchronized retries recreate the outage they respond to.

Watch out layered retries multiply (3 layers × 3 attempts = 27 calls); pick one layer to be the retrier.

Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter · AWS
Builds on The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing, Circuit Breaker, Idempotency & Idempotency Keys

Circuit Breaker

Michael Nygard · Release It! · 2007

Wrap calls to a failing dependency; after a failure threshold the breaker opens and calls fail fast without contacting the victim, then a half-open probe tests recovery.

Use when persistent downstream failure: retrying into a dying service finishes it off; breakers shed that load.

Watch out decide what an open breaker returns (error, fallback, cached value); that choice is the actual UX of the outage.

CircuitBreaker · FowlerRelease It!
Builds on The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing Leads to Timeouts, Retries & Backoff with Jitter, Bulkhead

Bulkhead

Nygard · Release It! · via Azure catalog

Partition resources (pools, threads, instances) so one consumer’s failure or saturation cannot drown the rest, like a ship’s watertight compartments.

Use when multi-tenant services and shared thread/connection pools; one noisy neighbor should sink one compartment only.

Watch out partitions cost utilization; size them from real load data, not symmetry.

Bulkhead · AzureWikipedia
Builds on Circuit Breaker

Idempotency & Idempotency Keys

Stripe’s API design canon

Safe retries require idempotent operations; for external side effects, the client sends a unique key so the server executes once and replays the stored result on retry.

Use when payments, order creation, webhooks, queue consumers: anywhere at-least-once delivery meets money or state.

Watch out key storage needs an expiry and a scope; ‘idempotent’ handlers that differ on the second call are the worst of both worlds.

Designing robust APIs with idempotency · StripeStripe API reference
Builds on The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing Leads to Timeouts, Retries & Backoff with Jitter

Queue-Based Load Leveling

Azure Architecture Center

Put a queue between producers and a service so bursts buffer instead of overwhelming it; the worker drains at its sustainable rate.

Use when spiky ingestion in front of steady processing: webhooks, uploads, batch jobs.

Watch out queues hide backpressure: bound the queue and surface lag as a first-class metric, or discover it as an outage.

Queue-Based Load Leveling · Azure

Throttling & Rate Limiting

Azure Architecture Center

Control resource consumption per client, tenant, or operation so demand spikes degrade service predictably instead of catastrophically.

Use when every public API and every shared internal resource; pairs with quotas and 429s clients can obey.

Watch out throttle with clear signals (retry-after); silent slowness teaches clients to retry harder.

Throttling · Azure

Testing

Test to buy confidence per unit of maintenance. Shape matters less than properties: deterministic, hermetic, mostly at the integration boundary, generated where inputs are wide.

Strategy

The Test Pyramid

Mike Cohn · popularized by Ham Vocke (martinfowler.com) · 2018

Write tests at different granularities; the higher the level, the fewer the tests. Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer service tests, fewest end-to-end.

Use when a default portfolio shape that keeps suites fast and failures local.

Watch out the ice-cream-cone inversion (mostly slow E2E tests) is “a nightmare to maintain”; also see the Trophy for UI-heavy apps.

Practical Test Pyramid · Vocke
Builds on Test-Driven Development Challenged by The Testing Trophy

The Testing Trophy

Guillermo Rauch (2016) · Kent C. Dodds

“Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.” Static analysis at the base, integration tests as the bulk; they exercise real collaboration with the best confidence-per-cost.

Use when apps where units are trivial but wiring is where bugs live (most web apps); coverage-chasing past ~70% has diminishing returns.

Watch out trophy vs pyramid is a portfolio argument, not a religion; libraries with deep pure logic still want a wide unit base.

Write tests · DoddsTesting Trophy
Challenges The Test Pyramid

Test-Driven Development

Kent Beck · TDD: By Example · 2002

Red–green–refactor: write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest thing, then clean up under green. The test is a design tool first, a regression net second.

Use when well-understood behavior with crisp examples; forces testable seams and tiny steps.

Watch out TDD on unclear requirements produces confident tests of the wrong thing; spike first, then test-drive.

Learning TDD · O’Reilly prefaceBeck · Goodreads
Builds on Do the Simplest Thing That Could Possibly Work Leads to The Test Pyramid, Don’t Mock What You Don’t Own, Spec-Driven Development Challenged by Is TDD Dead?

Technique

Property-Based Testing

Claessen & Hughes · QuickCheck · ICFP 2000

State invariants (‘for all inputs, decode(encode(x)) = x’) and let the framework generate and shrink counterexamples, instead of hand-picking examples.

Use when pure logic, parsers, serializers, anything with round-trips, orderings, or algebraic laws.

Watch out weak properties pass everything; the craft is in the invariant, and shrinking quality decides debuggability.

QuickCheck paper (PDF)PBT frameworks overview
Leads to Fuzzing

Mutation Testing

Stryker / PIT tooling

Inject small code mutations and check that tests fail; surviving mutants expose assertions you never actually made. Tests the tests.

Use when auditing a suite you’re about to trust for a refactor; coverage says code ran, mutation says behavior was checked.

Watch out expensive to run; target changed code or critical modules rather than the world.

Stryker · docs

Fuzzing

Google OSS-Fuzz · continuous fuzzing at scale

Feed generated and mutated inputs to anything that parses untrusted bytes, watching for crashes, hangs, and sanitizer violations.

Use when parsers, decoders, protocol handlers: the code attackers reach first. OSS-Fuzz exists because this finds real CVEs continuously.

Watch out fuzzing finds robustness bugs, not logic bugs; pair with property tests for semantics.

OSS-Fuzz
Builds on Property-Based Testing

Discipline

Hermetic, Deterministic Tests

Google Testing Blog

Tests control their world (fake time, network, randomness, and shared state) so a failure means the code changed, not the weather. A flaky test is a defect, not a nuisance.

Use when as a hard gate: quarantine or fix flakes immediately; a suite people retry is a suite people ignore.

Watch out sleeps and real clocks are the top flake sources; inject the clock.

Flaky tests at GoogleWhere flaky tests come from

Don’t Mock What You Don’t Own

Freeman & Pryce · GOOS

Mocking third-party interfaces verifies your guess about them; instead wrap the dependency in your own small interface, mock the wrapper, and integration-test the real thing.

Use when HTTP clients, SDKs, ORMs; the wrapper is also your anti-corruption layer.

Watch out a mock-everything suite can pass while production burns; every mocked boundary needs one real test somewhere.

What to mock · HynekFindmypast Tech
Builds on Test-Driven Development

Regression Test per Bug

Standard practice

Every bug fix ships with a test that failed before the fix and passes after: the bug’s tombstone.

Use when non-negotiable ritual; bugs cluster, and the second occurrence of a fixed bug is a process failure.

Watch out write the test first and watch it fail, or you may be enshrining a test that never detected anything.

Test Doubles & Service Stubs

Fowler · PoEAA (Service Stub)

Stand-ins (stubs, fakes, mocks) that remove dependence on slow or problematic services during testing; PoEAA canonized the Service Stub for exactly this.

Use when fast unit and integration tests; a good in-memory fake of your own gateway is worth a hundred mocks.

Watch out doubles drift from reality; contract tests or periodic real-service runs keep them honest.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Security

Deny by default and assume hostile input. Most of this section is fifty years old and still routinely violated, which is exactly why it stays in the canon.

Foundations

Saltzer & Schroeder’s Design Principles

Saltzer & Schroeder · 1975

The 1975 octet still underneath everything: economy of mechanism, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least privilege, least common mechanism, psychological acceptability.

Use when security design reviews: fifty years old and each principle still names a current breach class.

Watch out ‘open design’ means no security through obscurity of mechanism; keys stay secret, algorithms don’t.

The Protection of Information · full paper
Leads to Fail-Safe Defaults / Fail Closed, Least Privilege, Input Validation & Output Encoding

Fail-Safe Defaults / Fail Closed

Saltzer & Schroeder · 1975 · echoed by OWASP

Base access on explicit permission; the default is no access, and errors deny rather than allow. OWASP: security controls “fail securely”.

Use when authorization paths, feature gates, error handlers: ask what happens when the check itself breaks.

Watch out fail-open sneaks in as ‘graceful degradation’; degrading auth gracefully is a breach.

Saltzer & SchroederOWASP checklist
Builds on Saltzer & Schroeder’s Design Principles

Least Privilege

Saltzer & Schroeder · 1975

Every program, user, token, and service operates with the minimum privileges required, so a compromise is bounded by construction.

Use when DB users per service, scoped API tokens, IAM roles, container capabilities: everywhere a credential exists.

Watch out privilege creep is the default direction of entropy; audit grants on a schedule, not on an incident.

Saltzer & Schroeder
Builds on Saltzer & Schroeder’s Design Principles Leads to Supply-Chain Hygiene

Practice

Input Validation & Output Encoding

OWASP Secure Coding Practices

Validate all input on a trusted system with allow-lists and canonicalization; encode all output for its destination context (HTML, SQL, shell, URL) with tested routines.

Use when the two halves of injection defense: validate what comes in, encode what goes out, per context.

Watch out validation is not encoding; clean-looking input can still be an XSS payload for a context you didn’t encode for.

OWASP Secure Coding checklist
Builds on Saltzer & Schroeder’s Design Principles Challenges Postel’s Law and Its Modern Reversal Leads to Parameterized Queries

Parameterized Queries

OWASP Secure Coding Practices

“Use strongly typed parameterized queries”: SQL structure and data travel separately, ending injection by construction; least-privilege DB accounts bound the blast radius.

Use when all database access; string-built SQL is a finding, not a style choice.

Watch out dynamic identifiers (table/column names) can’t be parameterized; allow-list those explicitly.

OWASP Secure Coding checklist
Builds on Input Validation & Output Encoding, The Stored-Program Computer

Secrets Hygiene

Twelve-Factor config + OWASP

Secrets live in the environment or a secret manager, never in code, repos, logs, or error messages; config is what varies between deploys, and credentials are config.

Use when a leaked repo should cost you embarrassment, not credentials.

Watch out environment variables leak through crash dumps and child processes; managers with rotation beat raw env for high-value keys.

Config · 12factor.netOWASP checklist
Builds on The Twelve-Factor App

Supply-Chain Hygiene

OpenSSF · lockfile-first guidance

Pin dependencies with lockfiles, audit and update deliberately, and treat the package ecosystem as untrusted input; the lockfile is the cheapest supply-chain defense you own.

Use when every project with a package manager, which is every project.

Watch out pinning without a cadence trades supply-chain risk for unpatched-CVE risk; automate the update PRs.

The lockfile · SemgrepOpenSSF supply chain
Builds on Least Privilege

Design Patterns

The classic 1994 Gamma–Helm–Johnson–Vlissides vocabulary, plus what came after it: in modern languages many of the 23 dissolve into functions, modules, and types, and newer catalogs (distributed systems, messaging, reactivity) cover the problems that hurt today. A pattern is a vocabulary word, not a goal: apply one when its exact tension appears, never to appear designed.

The classic catalog

The Gang of Four Catalog

Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides · 1994

Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software: 23 patterns in three families (creational, structural, behavioral), plus the two meta-principles: program to an interface, and favor composition over inheritance.

Use when as vocabulary: a shared name compresses a design conversation from an hour to a sentence.

Watch out patterns are remedies for specific tensions, several of which dissolve in languages with closures and first-class functions; pattern-density is not design quality.

Design Patterns · WikipediaCatalog · refactoring.guru
Leads to Composition over Inheritance, Program to an Interface, not an Implementation, Enterprise Integration Patterns Challenged by Norvig: Patterns as Missing Language Features, Kay's OOP Isn't Java's OOP

Creational

Factory Method

GoF · 1994

Creates objects without specifying the exact class: subclasses (or implementations) decide what to instantiate behind a common creation interface.

Use when a framework must construct things whose concrete type its callers choose: plugins, drivers, per-format handlers.

Watch out one static create() with a switch is often enough; reach for the full pattern only when creation truly varies by subtype.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Abstract Factory

GoF · 1994

Groups factories that share a theme, producing whole families of related objects that are guaranteed to be mutually compatible.

Use when products come in consistent families: themed widgets, per-database driver sets, per-platform toolkits.

Watch out adding a new product type touches every factory; heavy unless the family axis is real and stable.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Builder

GoF · 1994

Constructs complex objects step by step, separating construction from representation so the same steps can yield different results.

Use when many optional parts, staged assembly, or fluent configuration of an immutable result.

Watch out in languages with named/default arguments and object literals, a builder is often ceremony.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Prototype

GoF · 1994

Creates new objects by cloning a configured exemplar instead of constructing from scratch.

Use when construction is expensive or the ‘recipe’ lives in runtime state; copy the configured instance.

Watch out deep-vs-shallow copy is the whole game; a shallow clone sharing mutable guts is a bug factory.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Singleton

GoF · 1994

Restricts a class to one instance with a global access point.

Use when a genuinely single physical resource: a process-wide config snapshot, a hardware handle.

Watch out the most regretted pattern: global mutable state in a costume, hostile to tests and concurrency. Prefer one instance created at the composition root and passed in.

Catalog · refactoring.guru
Challenged by Dependency Injection & the Composition Root

Structural

Adapter

GoF · 1994

Lets classes with incompatible interfaces work together by wrapping one to present the interface the other expects.

Use when integrating third-party or legacy types into your own interfaces; the in-process cousin of the anti-corruption layer.

Watch out adapters that add behavior stop being adapters; keep translation and logic separate.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Bridge

GoF · 1994

Decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two hierarchies can vary independently.

Use when two independent axes of variation (shapes × renderers, notifications × channels) threaten a class-per-combination explosion.

Watch out speculative bridges are indirection without payoff; wait until the second axis actually exists.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Composite

GoF · 1994

Composes objects into tree structures so individual items and whole groups are handled through one interface.

Use when part–whole hierarchies (UI trees, file systems, org charts) where callers shouldn’t care if it’s a leaf or a branch.

Watch out operations that only make sense on leaves (or only on groups) start sprouting type checks; keep the shared interface honest.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Decorator

GoF · 1994

Wraps an object to add behavior dynamically while preserving its interface: stackable, at runtime, per instance.

Use when optional, combinable add-ons: compression + encryption + buffering around a stream; middleware is this pattern.

Watch out deep decorator stacks are hard to debug and identity-sensitive code (equality, casts) breaks through wrappers.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Facade

GoF · 1994

Provides one simplified interface to a large subsystem, hiding its internal choreography.

Use when a messy or powerful subsystem needs a simple front door for the 90% use case; this is how you build Ousterhout’s deep modules.

Watch out a facade that merely re-exports everything hides nothing; keep the escape hatch to the full subsystem explicit.

Catalog · refactoring.guru
Leads to API Gateway & Backends for Frontends

Flyweight

GoF · 1994

Shares immutable intrinsic state among many objects to cut memory for huge object counts.

Use when millions of similar small objects (glyphs, map tiles, particles) where per-instance state is tiny.

Watch out an optimization pattern: measure first, and keep shared state strictly immutable.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Proxy

GoF · 1994

A stand-in with the same interface that controls access to the real object: lazily creating it, caching, guarding, or crossing a network.

Use when lazy loading, access control, remote objects, caching; the client shouldn’t know or care.

Watch out proxies change performance and failure semantics invisibly (Hyrum’s Law applies); document what the stand-in adds.

Catalog · refactoring.guru
Leads to Sidecar & Ambassador

Behavioral

Chain of Responsibility

GoF · 1994

Passes a request along a chain of handlers until one handles it, decoupling sender from receiver.

Use when layered handling: middleware pipelines, event bubbling, support-tier escalation.

Watch out requests can fall off the end unhandled; define the chain’s default explicitly.

Catalog · refactoring.guru
Leads to Middleware Pipelines

Command

GoF · 1994

Reifies an action and its parameters as an object that can be queued, logged, undone, or scheduled.

Use when undo/redo stacks, job queues, transactional scripts, macro recording.

Watch out in functional languages a closure is a command; add the class only when you need undo metadata or persistence.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Interpreter

GoF · 1994

Represents a small language’s grammar as a class hierarchy and evaluates sentences by walking the tree.

Use when a genuine mini-language (filters, rules, formulas) small enough to own.

Watch out grammars grow; past a modest size reach for a parser generator or an embedded language instead.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Iterator

GoF · 1994

Accesses a collection’s elements sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.

Use when already built into most languages (for…of, generators); implement the protocol for your own containers and lazy sequences.

Watch out mutation during iteration is the classic trap; define and enforce the policy.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Mediator

GoF · 1994

Centralizes many-to-many communication: colleagues talk to a mediator instead of each other, collapsing the interaction web into a hub.

Use when dialogs, form orchestration, chat rooms: n² pairwise coupling refactors into n spokes.

Watch out the mediator happily grows into a god object; keep it routing, not deciding everything.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Memento

GoF · 1994

Captures an object’s state in an opaque token so it can be restored later without violating encapsulation.

Use when undo, snapshots, transactional rollback of in-memory state.

Watch out snapshots of large state get expensive; consider event-sourced or persistent data structures instead.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Observer

GoF · 1994

Publish/subscribe: observers register with a subject and are notified of state changes, decoupling producers from consumers.

Use when UI data-binding, domain events, reactive streams: one change, many interested parties.

Watch out hidden control flow: cascades of notifications are hard to trace, leaked subscriptions are the classic memory leak, and ordering is undefined unless you define it.

Catalog · refactoring.guru
Leads to Domain Events & Messaging, Observables, Streams & Signals

State

GoF · 1994

An object alters its behavior when its internal state changes by delegating to a state object per mode, the OO rendering of a state machine.

Use when mode-dependent behavior drowning in flag checks; each state becomes a class, transitions become explicit.

Watch out pairs beautifully with ‘make illegal states unrepresentable’: model transitions as data, forbid the impossible ones at compile time.

Catalog · refactoring.guru
Builds on Statecharts

Strategy

GoF · 1994

Encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, selected at runtime.

Use when the same job done different ways (pricing rules, retry policies, compression codecs) chosen by config or context.

Watch out in functional languages this is ‘pass a function’; add the interface only when strategies carry state or need discovery.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Template Method

GoF · 1994

A base class defines an algorithm’s skeleton; subclasses fill in specific steps without changing its structure.

Use when a fixed workflow with pluggable steps, enforced by the framework (‘don’t call us, we’ll call you’).

Watch out inheritance-based variation inherits inheritance’s problems; Strategy-by-composition is usually the more flexible sibling.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Visitor

GoF · 1994

Separates operations from the object structure they operate on, letting you add new operations without touching the element classes.

Use when stable structure, growing operations: compilers walking ASTs are the canonical case.

Watch out the inverse trade: adding a new element type touches every visitor. Sum types with exhaustive matching serve the same need more simply.

Catalog · refactoring.guru

Modern successors

Norvig: Patterns as Missing Language Features

Peter Norvig · 1996

Norvig's famous finding: 16 of the 23 GoF patterns become invisible or radically simpler in dynamic languages. A pattern you keep re-implementing can be a sign your language lacks a feature, not a sign of good design.

Use when reading any pattern: ask which language feature would dissolve it (first-class functions dissolve Strategy and Command; modules dissolve Singleton).

Watch out ‘simpler in Lisp’ does not mean ‘unnecessary in Java’; the pattern still names a real tension in languages that have it.

Design Patterns in Dynamic Programming (PDF)c2 discussion
Challenges The Gang of Four Catalog Leads to Functional Replacements for GoF

Functional Replacements for GoF

Scott Wlaschin · “Functional Programming Design Patterns”

Wlaschin's mapping of the catalog onto core FP: Strategy and Command become plain functions, Decorator becomes function composition, Iterator becomes lazy sequences, Visitor becomes pattern matching over sum types.

Use when working in TypeScript, Rust, Kotlin, or F#: reach for the language feature before the class diagram.

Watch out FP has its own pattern vocabulary (functors, monads, folds); the complexity moves, it doesn't vanish.

fppatterns · WlaschinTalk · InfoQ
Builds on Norvig: Patterns as Missing Language Features

Dependency Injection & the Composition Root

Martin Fowler · 2004

Fowler's essay named the pattern that replaced Singleton and Service Locator: components declare their dependencies, and one composition root assembles the object graph (constructor injection preferred).

Use when everywhere, with or without a framework; DI without a container is just passing arguments in one well-chosen place.

Watch out containers can hide the object graph they were meant to clarify; magic resolution is Service Locator wearing a costume.

Inversion of Control Containers and the DI patternIoC · Wikipedia
Builds on Program to an Interface, not an Implementation Challenges Singleton Leads to Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)

Statecharts

David Harel · Science of Computer Programming · 1987

Harel extended finite state machines with hierarchy, orthogonal (parallel) regions, and history: the State pattern industrialized. XState and SCXML are direct descendants.

Use when UI and workflow logic beyond a handful of states; nested and parallel states end the boolean-flag explosion.

Watch out keep charts visualizable; a statechart nobody can read is a nested if wearing a diagram.

Statecharts: A Visual Formalism (PDF)Learning statecharts with XState
Leads to State

Observables, Streams & Signals

ReactiveX lineage → TC39 Signals proposal

Observer evolved twice: Rx-style observables added composition, cancellation, and backpressure to event streams; fine-grained signals (Solid, Vue, Angular, and a TC39 proposal) track dependencies automatically for derived state.

Use when streams for events over time; signals for current values that other values derive from. Manual subscribe/unsubscribe Observer is the leak factory both replace.

Watch out picking streams for state or signals for event firehoses recreates the original mess; the TC39 proposal is still in flux (status as of mid-2026: not yet standard).

Backpressure · ReactiveXtc39/proposal-signals
Builds on Observer

Middleware Pipelines

Express/Koa lineage

Chain of Responsibility modernized: an ordered pipeline of small (context, next) functions handling cross-cutting request concerns. The de facto architecture of every web framework.

Use when auth, logging, parsing, rate limiting; middleware ordering is real architecture, so document it.

Watch out middlemen couple invisibly through the shared context; one middleware that swallows errors silently breaks the whole chain.

KoaBasic middleware pattern in JS
Builds on Chain of Responsibility, The Unix Philosophy

Patterns of Distributed Systems

Unmesh Joshi · Fowler Signature Series

The modern heir to the catalog tradition: Write-Ahead Log, Quorum, Leader election, Versioned Value, Idempotent Receiver, documented from real systems like Kafka, etcd, and Cassandra.

Use when when today's hard problems are distributed, this is the pattern language to check before inventing your own consensus.

Watch out these patterns compose subtly; copying one without its stated prerequisites (ordering, durability) ships a bug with a famous name.

Catalog · martinfowler.comBook
Builds on Enterprise Integration Patterns, The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing

Enterprise Integration Patterns

Gregor Hohpe & Bobby Woolf · 2003

The messaging catalog: channels, routers, translators, splitters, aggregators, dead-letter queues. Still the shared vocabulary behind Kafka-era integration and every broker since.

Use when designing anything message-driven; the 65 patterns name what you will otherwise rediscover the hard way.

Watch out written in the ESB era; the patterns survive, but centralized smart-pipe architectures they rode in on mostly did not (smart endpoints, dumb pipes).

enterpriseintegrationpatterns.comBook page · Fowler
Builds on The Gang of Four Catalog Leads to Domain Events & Messaging, Patterns of Distributed Systems, MCP: Model Context Protocol

Architecture

How systems are shaped: domain logic, persistence, service boundaries, and the distributed patterns that keep many machines coherent. Every pattern here trades simplicity for a specific capability; pay the complexity only when its problem has actually arrived.

Styles & boundaries

Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)

Alistair Cockburn

The application core exposes ports (interfaces it defines); adapters plug the world (UI, DB, queues, tests) into those ports. Inside knows nothing about outside.

Use when you want the core testable without infrastructure and swappable edges; kin to onion/clean architecture and functional core, imperative shell.

Watch out for CRUD-thin apps the ceremony can exceed the core; the payoff scales with domain logic.

Hexagonal architecture · CockburnWikipedia
Builds on Program to an Interface, not an Implementation, Dependency Injection & the Composition Root Leads to Functional Core, Imperative Shell, MCP: Model Context Protocol

Functional Core, Imperative Shell

Gary Bernhardt · Destroy All Software

Pure decision-making logic lives in a functional core; a thin imperative shell owns all I/O and feeds the core values in, effects out. Bernhardt's screencast and “Boundaries” talk made it canon.

Use when the small-scale sibling of hexagonal: most unit tests hit the pure core with plain values, and the shell stays too thin to hide bugs.

Watch out a shell that starts making decisions (or a core that sneaks in a clock or a network call) quietly dissolves the whole benefit.

Functional Core, Imperative Shell · screencastBoundaries · talk
Builds on Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)

Model–View–Controller

Trygve Reenskaug lineage · PoEAA formulation

“Splits user interface interaction into three distinct roles”: model holds state and logic, view renders, controller mediates input.

Use when the ancestral separation behind nearly every UI framework; the enduring lesson is keeping domain logic out of the view.

Watch out ‘MVC’ means something different in every framework; agree on which one before arguing about it.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler
Leads to Front Controller

Front Controller

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

One controller handles all requests for a site; the single entry point where routing, auth, and cross-cutting concerns live; every modern web framework’s router is one.

Use when consolidating cross-cutting request logic instead of duplicating it per page.

Watch out middleware ordering in the front controller becomes real architecture; document it.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler
Builds on Model–View–Controller

Transaction Script vs Domain Model

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

Two ways to organize business logic: a procedure per request (Transaction Script) or an object model where data and behavior live together (Domain Model).

Use when scripts for simple, mostly-CRUD logic; a domain model when rules are rich, interrelated, and reused across operations.

Watch out the classic failure is the ‘anemic domain model’: model-shaped classes with script-shaped logic smeared elsewhere.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler
Leads to Anemic Domain Model

Service Layer

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

“Defines an application’s boundary with a layer of services that establishes a set of available operations”; the API of your domain, coordinating workflows and transactions.

Use when multiple clients (web, jobs, API) need the same operations with the same rules; the layer is where use-cases live.

Watch out a service layer that only forwards to repositories is a corridor; put orchestration there or don’t build it.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Domain-Driven Boundaries (Subdomains & Contexts)

Eric Evans’s DDD · applied by microservices.io

Partition a large domain by business subdomains, each with its own model and language; integrate contexts deliberately (e.g., through anti-corruption layers) rather than sharing one grand model.

Use when decomposing services or teams: ‘decompose by business capability / subdomain’ is the microservices boundary heuristic that survives contact with reality.

Watch out boundaries drawn by org chart or database tables instead of the domain produce distributed monoliths; see Conway.

Decomposition patterns · microservices.ioACL · Azure
Builds on High Cohesion, Low Coupling, Conway’s Law Leads to Anti-Corruption Layer, Database per Service

Monolith First, Microservices Maybe

Chris Richardson · microservices.io framing

Monolith and microservices are both legitimate styles with explicit trade-offs: one deployable unit and simple operations vs. independent deployability, scaling, and team autonomy, paid for with all eight distributed-computing fallacies.

Use when split when team scale, deploy contention, or divergent scaling actually hurt, and split along subdomain seams.

Watch out microservices are an organizational scaling tool more than a technical one; a distributed system you didn’t need is pure cost (see Gall’s Law).

Patterns index · microservices.io
Builds on Gall’s Law, Conway’s Law Leads to The Monolith Strikes Back

Domain & persistence (PoEAA)

Repository

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

“Mediates between the domain and data mapping layers using a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects”: the domain asks for aggregates, not rows.

Use when a rich domain model that must stay persistence-ignorant; also the natural seam for in-memory fakes in tests.

Watch out generic repository<T> wrappers over an ORM add nothing; repositories earn their keep exposing domain-meaningful queries.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Unit of Work

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

“Maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates the writing out of changes”: one commit, correct ordering, no partial writes.

Use when multiple objects change together and must persist atomically; your ORM’s session/context is one.

Watch out long-lived units of work hold locks and stale state; scope them to the business transaction, no wider.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Active Record vs Data Mapper

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

Active Record: the object wraps a row and saves itself: simple, fast to build. Data Mapper: “a layer of mappers that moves data between objects and a database while keeping them independent.”

Use when Active Record for CRUD apps whose model mirrors tables; Data Mapper when the domain model must diverge from the schema.

Watch out Active Record couples domain to persistence by design: fine until the domain gets rich, painful after.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Identity Map & Lazy Load

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

Identity Map “ensures that each object gets loaded only once” per session; Lazy Load defers fetching data until first use.

Use when the machinery inside every serious ORM; know them to understand what your ORM is doing to you.

Watch out lazy loading in a loop is the N+1 query generator; identity maps make stale reads possible across long sessions.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Gateway, Remote Facade & DTO

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

Gateway encapsulates access to an external system; Remote Facade provides a coarse-grained face over fine-grained objects; the DTO “carries data between processes to reduce the number of method calls.”

Use when the trio that makes process boundaries livable: chunky calls, explicit payloads, wrapped externals.

Watch out DTO-mapping boilerplate is real; generate it or scope it to actual process boundaries, not every layer.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Special Case (Null Object)

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

“A subclass that provides special behavior for particular cases”: e.g., a MissingCustomer that behaves sensibly instead of a null that must be checked everywhere.

Use when a domain concept has a meaningful ‘absent/default’ behavior; callers stop branching on null.

Watch out a special case that silently absorbs writes hides bugs; it must behave correctly, not just not-crash.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Optimistic vs Pessimistic Offline Lock

Fowler · PoEAA · 2002

Across long business transactions: optimistic locking detects conflicts at commit and rolls back; pessimistic locking prevents them by letting only one transaction touch the data at a time.

Use when optimistic when conflicts are rare (web apps, version columns); pessimistic when redoing work is unacceptable or conflicts are common.

Watch out optimistic locking without a user-facing merge/retry story just moves the failure to the save button.

PoEAA catalog · Fowler

Distributed & cloud

API Gateway & Backends for Frontends

microservices.io · Azure catalog

A single entry point for clients (gateway), optionally with one purpose-built backend per frontend type (BFF), handling routing, aggregation, auth, and offloaded cross-cutting concerns.

Use when many services behind many clients; BFF when web, mobile, and partners need genuinely different shapes.

Watch out the gateway is a chokepoint and a deploy bottleneck if it accretes business logic; keep it thin.

API gateway · microservices.ioGateway patterns · Azure
Builds on Facade

Database per Service

Chris Richardson · microservices.io

Each service owns its data store exclusively; others get data through its API, never its tables. The alternative (shared database) couples every service at the schema.

Use when real service autonomy: independent schemas, scaling, and deploys. This is the decision that makes microservices micro.

Watch out you just signed up for distributed data: sagas, outboxes, and eventual consistency are the bill.

Database per service · microservices.io
Builds on Domain-Driven Boundaries (Subdomains & Contexts) Leads to Saga

Saga

microservices.io · Azure catalog

Manages consistency across services without distributed transactions: a sequence of local transactions, each publishing the next step, with compensating transactions to undo on failure.

Use when multi-service workflows (order → payment → inventory) once two-phase commit is off the table.

Watch out compensations are not rollbacks: design each step to be compensatable, and expect to observe in-between states.

Saga · microservices.ioSaga · Azure
Builds on Database per Service Leads to Transactional Outbox

Transactional Outbox

Chris Richardson · microservices.io

Write the domain change and the event to publish in one local transaction (the outbox table); a relay publishes events afterwards: atomically consistent messaging without 2PC.

Use when any ‘save to DB and publish to broker’ pair; without it, one of the two will eventually happen alone.

Watch out the relay must be idempotent and ordered per aggregate; consumers still need dedupe (at-least-once delivery).

Transactional outbox · microservices.io
Builds on Saga, Domain Events & Messaging

CQRS

Greg Young · documented by Fowler · Azure catalog

Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate models for updating and reading: commands mutate a write model, queries hit read models shaped for each view.

Use when read and write workloads differ wildly, or complex domains need simple, fast, denormalized views; often paired with event sourcing.

Watch out Fowler’s documented caution: most systems don’t need it; apply CQRS to a bounded context that has earned it, never as a whole-app default.

CQRS · FowlerCQRS · Azure
Builds on Command–Query Separation Leads to Event Sourcing

Event Sourcing

Azure catalog · microservices.io

“Use an append-only store to record a full series of events that describe actions taken on data”: current state is a fold over history, and history is the source of truth.

Use when audit is a first-class requirement, temporal queries matter, or events already are the domain (ledgers, trading).

Watch out schema evolution of old events, replay cost, and GDPR-style deletion are the long-tail bills; snapshotting is not optional at scale.

Event Sourcing · AzureEvent sourcing · microservices.io
Builds on CQRS

Domain Events & Messaging

microservices.io

Services publish facts (‘OrderPlaced’) rather than calling each other’s verbs; consumers react asynchronously, decoupling availability and deploy schedules.

Use when cross-service side effects (notifications, projections, integrations) where temporal coupling would hurt.

Watch out async trades latency coupling for eventual consistency and observability debt: you now need tracing, DLQs, and idempotent consumers.

Messaging & domain events · microservices.io
Builds on Observer, Enterprise Integration Patterns Leads to Transactional Outbox

Service Discovery

Chris Richardson · microservices.io

Services find each other through a registry, client-side (caller queries registry, picks instance) or server-side (a router/LB does it), instead of hardcoded addresses.

Use when dynamic fleets where instances come and go; in Kubernetes, the platform’s DNS/service layer is this pattern operated for you.

Watch out discovery data is a cache of reality; health checks and TTLs decide how wrong it can briefly be.

Service discovery · microservices.io
Builds on The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing

Sidecar & Ambassador

Azure Architecture Center

Deploy helper functionality in a companion process/container: sidecars add capabilities (proxying, telemetry, config) beside the app; ambassadors specifically proxy its outbound network calls.

Use when cross-cutting infrastructure (mTLS, retries, metrics) applied uniformly without touching app code; service meshes are sidecars industrialized.

Watch out each sidecar adds latency, resources, and a failure mode; a mesh is a platform commitment, not a sprinkle.

Sidecar · AzureAmbassador · Azure
Builds on Proxy

Strangler Fig

Martin Fowler · via Azure catalog

Incrementally replace a legacy system by routing functionality piece by piece to new services around it, until the old system is strangled and removed.

Use when the escape from big-bang rewrites Gall’s Law warns about: value ships continuously and risk stays bounded.

Watch out needs an interception seam (proxy, facade) and the discipline to finish; half-strangled systems are two systems forever.

Strangler Fig · FowlerStrangler Fig · Azure
Builds on Gall’s Law, Big Ball of Mud

Cache-Aside

Azure Architecture Center

“Load data on demand into a cache from a data store”: on miss, read the store, populate the cache; on write, update the store and invalidate.

Use when read-heavy data that tolerates brief staleness; the simplest honest caching strategy.

Watch out you have now acquired the first Hard Thing: invalidation, stampedes, and staleness windows are yours to bound (TTLs, single-flight).

Cache-Aside · Azure

Sharding

Azure Architecture Center

“Divide a data store into a set of horizontal partitions or shards”, each holding a subset keyed by a shard key.

Use when a dataset or write load that one node genuinely cannot hold, once vertical scaling and read replicas are exhausted.

Watch out the shard key is nearly unchangeable later; hot keys and cross-shard queries are the failure modes to design against first.

Sharding · Azure

Richardson Maturity Model

Leonard Richardson · explained by Fowler

Levels of REST adoption: level 0, one URI tunnel; level 1, resources; level 2, HTTP verbs and status codes; level 3, hypermedia controls (HATEOAS).

Use when a shared ruler for API design conversations; level 2 is the industry’s working plateau.

Watch out maturity is not a mandate; level 3’s payoff depends on clients that actually follow links, which most don’t.

Richardson Maturity Model · Fowler
Builds on REST-as-Practiced Isn't Fielding's REST

MCP: Model Context Protocol

Anthropic · November 2024 · open standard

An open protocol connecting AI assistants to tools and data, pitched as “a USB-C port for AI applications”: one adapter contract instead of N×M custom integrations, and industry-adopted within a year.

Use when exposing systems to agents: it is ports-and-adapters for the AI era, so least privilege, schema validation, and idempotency apply to every tool you publish.

Watch out a protocol standardizes plumbing, not judgment: each MCP tool is a live trust boundary carrying prompt-injection and privilege risk.

Introducing MCP · AnthropicMCP · Wikipedia
Builds on Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters), Enterprise Integration Patterns Leads to Harness Engineering

Delivery & Ops

How working software keeps working: small safe changes, evidence-based delivery metrics, deliberate documentation, and operations you can observe.

Shipping

The Twelve-Factor App

Heroku (Adam Wiggins) · 12factor.net

Twelve rules for deployable services; the load-bearing ones: config in the environment, stateless processes, dev/prod parity, logs as event streams, disposability.

Use when the default contract for anything that runs in a container; factor III (config) alone prevents a class of leaks and snowflakes.

Watch out written for Heroku-era PaaS; treat as principles, not scripture; some factors (e.g., logs to stdout) assume a platform that catches them.

Config · 12factor.net
Leads to Secrets Hygiene

Semantic Versioning

Tom Preston-Werner · semver.org

MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: increment MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes.

Use when any published interface: libraries, APIs, schemas; the version number is a compressed changelog of risk.

Watch out Hyrum’s Law: consumers depend on behavior you never promised, so ‘compatible’ is an aspiration to verify, not declare.

semver.orgHyrum’s Law
Leads to Conventional Commits

Parallel Change (Expand → Migrate → Contract)

Danilo Sato on Fowler’s bliki · technique via Kerievsky

Never break readers in one step: add the new form alongside the old (expand), move consumers over (migrate), then remove the old (contract).

Use when schema changes, API evolution, renames: anything with independent deploy timing between writers and readers.

Watch out the contract step is the one teams skip; un-contracted expansions accumulate as permanent double-writes.

Parallel Change · Fowler bliki

Feature Flags & Kill Switches

Pete Hodgson · martinfowler.com

Toggle behavior at runtime to decouple deploy from release: gradual rollouts, A/B exposure, and instant kill switches for misbehaving paths.

Use when risky launches and trunk-based development; the flag is how unfinished code ships safely.

Watch out flags are inventory with a carrying cost: categorize by lifespan and delete released ones, or inherit 2^n untested configurations.

Feature Toggles · Hodgson
Leads to Trunk-Based Development

Trunk-Based Development

trunkbaseddevelopment.com

Everyone integrates into one shared trunk in small, frequent commits; branches, if any, live hours to a couple of days behind flags.

Use when continuous integration in the literal sense: merge pain shrinks with batch size; DORA’s data associates the practice with elite delivery.

Watch out requires the safety net first: fast CI, good tests, feature flags. Trunk-based without them is just pushing to main.

trunkbaseddevelopment.comShort-lived branches
Builds on If It Hurts, Do It More Often, Feature Flags & Kill Switches Leads to DORA’s Four Keys

Conventional Commits

conventionalcommits.org

A commit-message convention (feat:, fix:, BREAKING CHANGE:) that makes history machine-readable: changelogs and semver bumps generate themselves.

Use when any repo wanting automated releases; the grammar costs nothing once habitual.

Watch out the type prefix doesn’t excuse the message body: say why, not just what kind.

Conventional Commits
Builds on Semantic Versioning

Code Review, the Google Way

Google Engineering Practices

Reviewers check design, functionality, complexity, tests, naming, comments, style, and docs, with small changelists and fast reviewer response as the enabling constraints.

Use when review for what tools can’t catch (design, clarity); let linters argue about formatting.

Watch out review standards that demand perfection stall delivery; the bar is ‘definitely improves code health’, not flawless.

Code review · Google eng-practices
Challenged by Vibe Coding

Knowledge

Architecture Decision Records

Michael Nygard · 2011

Short, numbered documents capturing each architecturally significant decision: context, decision, consequences; stored with the code, immutable once accepted.

Use when any decision a future maintainer will ask ‘why on earth…’ about; ADRs are Chesterton’s fences with the reason written on them.

Watch out ADRs record decisions, not designs; keep them one page and write them when the decision happens, not archaeologically.

Documenting Architecture Decisions · Nygardadr.github.io
Builds on Technical Debt

Diátaxis

Daniele Procida · diataxis.fr

Documentation has four distinct jobs: tutorials (learning), how-to guides (tasks), reference (information), and explanation (understanding). Mixing them is why docs disappoint.

Use when structuring any docs site; most ‘bad docs’ are one type wearing another’s clothes.

Watch out don’t force four sections on day one; classify what users actually need first, then fill the grid.

Diátaxis

Operating

DORA’s Four Keys

DORA / Accelerate research program

Evidence-based delivery metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore. Speed and stability, measured together, correlate rather than trade off.

Use when measuring the delivery system, not the developers; improving the four keys means removing friction, not pressuring people.

Watch out Goodhart applies the moment keys become targets per team; use them as a flashlight, not a whip.

DORA metrics · dora.devFour Keys · Google Cloud
Builds on Trunk-Based Development, The Agile Manifesto’s Four Values Leads to AI Pair Programming Meets the Evidence

SRE: Golden Signals, SLOs & Error Budgets

Google SRE Book

Monitor latency, traffic, errors, and saturation; define Service Level Objectives users actually feel, and spend the error budget (the allowed unreliability) on shipping.

Use when the framework that turns ‘is it up?’ into an engineering budget: too many incidents, freeze features; budget to spare, take risks.

Watch out SLOs on metrics users don’t feel produce theater; alert on symptoms (the signals), page on budget burn.

Monitoring Distributed Systems · SRE Book
Leads to Blameless Postmortems

Canonical Log Lines

Stripe engineering

Emit one wide, structured log event per unit of work (request, job, transaction) carrying all key dimensions, so most questions are one query, not a join across scattered lines.

Use when the highest-leverage observability practice per line of code; pairs with tracing, replaces log spelunking.

Watch out never log secrets or PII into the wide event: it is precisely the record everyone can query.

Canonical log lines · Stripe

Performance & Concurrency

Measure before optimizing, bound what you parallelize, and prefer structure over cleverness in concurrent code.

Performance

Measure First

Knuth’s 3% · the profiling discipline

Optimize only what a profiler names: the critical ~3% is real but never where intuition points. Everything else stays simple.

Use when any performance work: the profile is the ticket of admission, and before/after numbers are the definition of done.

Watch out microbenchmarks lie (JIT, caches, dead-code elimination); measure the real workload where possible.

Knuth in context · hlopko
Builds on Knuth: Premature Optimization Leads to Clean Code Under Fire

Amdahl’s Law

Gene Amdahl · 1967

Speedup from parallelizing is capped by the serial fraction: if 10% must run serially, infinite cores still top out at 10×.

Use when before scaling out: find and shrink the serial fraction (locks, single queues, coordination); that is where the ceiling lives.

Watch out applies per workload, and coordination overhead makes real curves worse than the formula’s optimism.

Amdahl’s law · Wikipedia

Concurrency

Share Memory by Communicating

Go proverb · go.dev

“Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating”: pass ownership of data through channels/messages so only one goroutine touches it at a time.

Use when designing concurrent code: ownership transfer replaces lock choreography; the type system or convention tracks who may touch what.

Watch out channels are not free and can deadlock too; for tiny critical sections a mutex is simpler and faster. The principle is about ownership clarity.

Share Memory By Communicating · Go blog

Structured Concurrency

Nathaniel J. Smith · “Go statement considered harmful” · 2018

Concurrent tasks live inside a scope that outlives none of them: children finish or cancel before the scope exits, so errors propagate and nothing leaks into the void.

Use when any spawned work: nurseries/task groups make cancellation, timeouts, and error handling composable instead of ad hoc.

Watch out fire-and-forget still exists at the edges (servers’ accept loops); model it as an explicitly owned long-lived scope, not an orphan.

Notes on structured concurrency · njs

Bound Everything

TigerStyle · Power of 10 rule 2

Every queue, pool, buffer, and loop gets a fixed upper bound; unbounded anything is a latent outage; backpressure is a feature you design, not an accident you discover.

Use when sizing any concurrent structure: pick the limit, define what happens at the limit (block, shed, degrade), and test at the limit.

Watch out a bound without a policy is just a different crash; the policy at saturation is the actual design decision.

TIGER_STYLE.mdPower of 10 (PDF)
Builds on TigerStyle, NASA’s Power of 10 Leads to Loop Engineering

Anti-Patterns & Rethinks

Named failure modes, and the places where the folklore contradicts its own sources. Anti-patterns are solutions that recur despite their negative consequences; rethinks are modern discoveries and re-readings that challenge the status quo. Both earn a card the same way: by showing up in real systems.

Named anti-patterns

Big Ball of Mud

Brian Foote & Joseph Yoder · 1997

“A haphazardly structured, sprawling, sloppy, duct-tape-and-baling-wire, spaghetti-code jungle.” The paper's uncomfortable thesis: this is the de facto standard architecture, because real forces (deadlines, turnover, growth) push toward it.

Spot it no discernible boundaries; every change touches everything; the architecture diagram is aspirational fiction.

Escape incremental consolidation along seams (strangler style); big-bang rewrites usually rebuild the mud with newer bricks (see Gall).

Big Ball of Mud · laputan.orgOriginal paper (PDF)
Leads to Strangler Fig

God Object (The Blob)

AntiPatterns · Brown, Malveau, McCormick & Mowbray · 1998

One class hoards most of the knowledge and behavior while everything else is a data bag; every feature request routes through the same thousand-line file.

Spot it a class named Manager, Processor, or Util that imports half the codebase and appears in every stack trace.

Escape extract along responsibilities using Information Expert; move behavior to the data it needs, one seam at a time.

AntiPatterns · ACMAnti-patterns overview · Wikibooks

Anemic Domain Model

Martin Fowler · 2003

Model-shaped classes with getters and setters but no behavior, while the logic lives in a layer of ‘service’ scripts. Fowler: it is “contrary to the basic idea of object-oriented design”.

Spot it entities that are pure data bags plus a service layer that reads like procedural code operating on them.

Escape move the behavior onto the model it belongs to; or admit the domain is simple and choose Transaction Script honestly.

AnemicDomainModel · FowlerWikipedia
Builds on Transaction Script vs Domain Model

Golden Hammer

AntiPatterns · 1998

“When all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail”: the team's favorite technology applied to every problem regardless of fit.

Spot it the same tool appears in every design regardless of the question; alternatives are dismissed without evaluation.

Escape spend innovation tokens deliberately (see Choose Boring Technology) and require one written alternative per big decision (an ADR forces this).

Anti-patterns overview · Wikibooks

Lava Flow

AntiPatterns · 1998

Dead code and forgotten experiments hardened into the codebase like cooled lava: nobody remembers why it exists, so nobody dares remove it.

Spot it commented-out blocks with fossil timestamps, unreachable branches, flags nobody flips, ‘temporary’ code with tenure.

Escape run Chesterton's fence forward: learn why it exists (git blame, tests), then delete boldly; version control remembers so your codebase doesn't have to.

Anti-patterns overview · Wikibooks

Distributed Monolith

Modern microservices folklore

Services that must deploy together, share a database, or call each other in synchronous chains: microservice operational cost with monolith coupling. The worst of both worlds.

Spot it a ‘simple’ change opens pull requests in four repos; one service's deploy breaks another; the ‘independent’ services share tables.

Escape database per service, async events, and honest boundaries; or merge back into a modular monolith and stop paying network tax for function calls.

Distributed monolith · vFunctionIs your microservice a distributed monolith? · Gremlin
Builds on The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing

Speculative Generality

Code smell · Fowler & Beck's Refactoring

Hooks, parameters, abstract classes, and plugin points built for futures that never arrive. YAGNI's shadow, cast in class hierarchies.

Spot it interfaces with one implementation, parameters always passed the same value, ‘extensibility’ nobody has extended.

Escape delete unused flexibility (version control remembers); reintroduce it at the third real use (rule of three).

Speculative Generality · refactoring.guru
Builds on YAGNI: You Aren’t Gonna Need It

Rethinks & reversals

Kay's OOP Isn't Java's OOP

Alan Kay · OOPSLA 1997 keynote · 2003 email to Stefan Ram

The man who coined the term: “OOP to me means only messaging, local retention and protection and hiding of state-process, and extreme late-binding of all things.” And: “I invented the term Object-Oriented, and I can tell you I did not have C++ in mind.” Class hierarchies and inheritance are the part he didn't mean.

Takeaway judge ‘OOP’ code by encapsulation and message-like boundaries, not class count; Erlang processes and actors are arguably closer to Kay's vision than Java class trees.

Nuance this is an argument about lineage and emphasis, not a proof that class-based OOP fails; Java-style OOP built a lot of working software.

Alan Kay and OO Programming · PoeThe big idea is messaging
Challenges The Gang of Four Catalog

The Banana, the Gorilla, and the Jungle

Joe Armstrong · Coders at Work

Armstrong on inheritance-heavy OOP: “you wanted a banana but what you got was a gorilla holding the banana and the entire jungle.” Implicit environment rides along with every inherited class.

Takeaway prefer explicit, minimal dependencies; note that Go and Rust shipped without implementation inheritance at all, and few miss it.

Nuance the quote targets entangled hierarchies, not objects as such; small, shallow, composed objects don't drag jungles.

You wanted a banana · John D. Cook
Builds on Composition over Inheritance

REST-as-Practiced Isn't Fielding's REST

Roy Fielding · 2008

Fielding, who defined REST in his dissertation, wrote “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven” and objected to HTTP+JSON RPC-style APIs calling themselves REST. Most ‘REST’ APIs sit at Richardson level 2 and ignore hypermedia entirely.

Takeaway name your style honestly (an HTTP API is a fine thing to build) and adopt hypermedia only where clients will actually follow links.

Nuance same species as the Kay case: a coined term drifted from its coiner. The drifted meaning won the industry; knowing both saves you from cargo-culting either.

REST APIs must be hypertext-driven · FieldingHATEOAS · Wikipedia
Leads to Richardson Maturity Model

Waterfall Was a Warning, Not a Recommendation

Winston Royce · 1970

The paper cited as waterfall's origin shows the single-pass diagram and immediately calls that implementation “risky and invites failure”, then recommends iteration, early prototyping (“do it twice”), and heavy customer involvement.

Takeaway the field adopted the strawman figure and skipped the caveats; read the primary source you cite (this page's whole reason for linking them).

Nuance Royce still valued documentation and upfront thinking far more than agile folklore admits; the paper fits neither camp's slogan.

Royce 1970 (PDF)Reading the original paper · pragtob
Challenged by The Agile Manifesto’s Four Values

Is TDD Dead?

DHH vs. Kent Beck & Martin Fowler · 2014

Heinemeier Hansson declared “TDD is dead. Long live testing.”, arguing test-first dogma produces test-induced design damage; Beck and Fowler answered in a recorded hangout series mapping where TDD earns its keep and where it distorts design.

Takeaway treat TDD as a tool with a domain (crisp units, evolving APIs) rather than a moral test; system-level tests are a legitimate primary strategy.

Nuance both sides agree on the destination (confidence, feedback); the fight is about the route. Dogma in either direction is the actual casualty.

TDD is dead. Long live testing. · DHHWas TDD ever alive?
Challenges Test-Driven Development

Clean Code Under Fire

qntm · Casey Muratori (2023)

qntm's close reading argues the book's own examples violate its rules and haven't aged well; Muratori benchmarked its polymorphism-and-tiny-functions advice at large multiples slower than data-oriented equivalents on numeric kernels.

Takeaway extract the durable core (meaningful names, small focused units, honest tests) and drop the absolutism; performance-sensitive code plays by measured rules, not style rules.

Nuance Muratori's numbers come from a compute kernel, the worst case for dynamic dispatch; most business code is bounded by I/O, not vtables. Context decides.

Stop recommending Clean Code · qntm“Clean” Code, Horrible Performance · Muratori
Builds on Measure First

CUPID over SOLID

Dan North · cupid.dev

North argues SOLID hardened into pass/fail dogma and proposes properties instead of principles: Composable, Unix philosophy, Predictable, Idiomatic, Domain-based. Properties grade on a spectrum; principles get argued about.

Takeaway use CUPID as a code-review lens (“how composable, how idiomatic?”) alongside SOLID rather than as a replacement religion.

Nuance CUPID trades SOLID's false precision for vagueness of its own; ‘joyful’ isn't checkable either. Both are conversation starters, not linters.

CUPID for joyful coding · Northcupid.dev
Challenges Single Responsibility Principle, Open–Closed Principle, Liskov Substitution Principle, Interface Segregation Principle, Dependency Inversion Principle

The Monolith Strikes Back

Fowler's Monolith First (2015) · Prime Video case (2023)

Fowler observed that almost all successful microservice systems started as monoliths, while systems built as microservices from scratch ended in trouble. In 2023, Amazon's Prime Video team merged a serverless microservice pipeline back into a monolith and reported roughly 90% infrastructure cost reduction, widely covered as a pendulum moment.

Takeaway distribution is a cost you pay for organizational scale and independent deployability, not a default architecture; modular monolith first, split at proven seams.

Nuance one team's workload isn't a universal verdict; the same report is also an argument for choosing the right compute model per workload.

MonolithFirst · FowlerPrime Video case coverage · DevClass (2023)
Builds on Monolith First, Microservices Maybe

The Typed-Language Evidence Fight

Ray et al. (FSE 2014) vs. Berger et al. (TOPLAS 2019)

A famous large-scale GitHub study associated functional and statically typed languages with fewer defects; a 2019 reproduction study failed to replicate most of the claims after correcting the methodology, and the original authors published a rebuttal in turn.

Takeaway treat ‘studies prove my language is better’ claims with source-critical care; empirical software engineering is young and effect sizes here were small either way.

Nuance failed replication of one study is not proof of the opposite claim; type systems still earn their keep in this canon on mechanism (compile-time proof), not on that correlation.

Reproduction study · TOPLAS 2019Original authors' rebuttal (arXiv)

The Agile Industrial Complex

Martin Fowler (2018) · Ron Jeffries (2018)

Fowler's State of Agile 2018 keynote names the Agile Industrial Complex: imposed frameworks, certified process, and tooling that invert the manifesto's first value. Jeffries, a manifesto signatory, advised developers to abandon capital-A ‘Agile’ and keep the ideas (his ‘dark scrum’ critique).

Takeaway when the framework outranks the people using it, the manifesto itself says you've lost; measure ceremonies by whether the team would keep them voluntarily.

Nuance the critique targets the industry around agile, not iteration, feedback, or the manifesto; throwing those out is overcorrection.

The State of Agile Software in 2018 · FowlerDevelopers Should Abandon Agile · Jeffries
Builds on The Agile Manifesto’s Four Values

AI Pair Programming Meets the Evidence

DORA · Accelerate State of DevOps 2024

DORA's 2024 report found rising AI adoption associated with gains in individual productivity and code quality perceptions, but with small decreases in software delivery throughput and stability: the tooling moved faster than the delivery discipline around it.

Takeaway AI-generated code rides your existing safety nets; strengthen review, tests, and small-batch delivery first, then scale the assistant (as of the 2024 report; this evidence base is moving fast).

Nuance correlational survey data, not a controlled experiment; later reports and better integration practices may (and likely will) shift the picture.

DORA 2024 reportThroughput & stability analysis · RedMonk
Builds on DORA’s Four Keys Leads to The METR Surprise, DORA 2025: AI as Amplifier

The METR Surprise

METR randomized controlled trial · July 2025

A randomized trial of experienced open-source maintainers working on their own repositories: with AI tools allowed, tasks took 19% longer, while participants estimated afterwards that AI had made them about 20% faster. The perception gap is the headline result.

Takeaway measure AI workflows against your own baseline instead of trusting felt speed; expert developers on familiar code are exactly where AI assistance is weakest.

Nuance one setting, early-2025 tools, expert maintainers on mature repos: METR itself cautions against generalizing and has since redesigned its follow-up experiments.

METR studyPaper (arXiv)
Builds on AI Pair Programming Meets the Evidence

DORA 2025: AI as Amplifier

DORA · State of AI-assisted Software Development · 2025

The follow-up report reframes the 2024 result: AI amplifies what an organization already is. Teams with strong platforms and small batches see gains; weak systems see their dysfunction amplified; and most developers report daily AI use alongside only moderate trust in its output.

Takeaway fix the delivery system first (the four keys still rule); AI multiplies your baseline in whichever direction it already points.

Nuance survey correlations again, in a fast-moving field: treat each year's report as a snapshot of practice, not settled physics.

DORA 2025 reportAI as amplifier · InfoQ
